column2: OpenClaw's lasting contribution is the self-hosted agent runtime pattern itself, which others copied, extended, and hardened within months.
Self-hosted Claw-pattern runtime that contains execution in Docker containers by design, instead of relying on configuration restrictions.
NanoClaw confines tool execution through architecture. OpenClaw starts with host access and depends on opt-in restrictions set in config.
Config hardening narrows but cannot remove the risk that an injected tool with filesystem access reaches anything the host process can.
Sensitive regulated data, several users needing isolation from each other, unreviewed community tools, or existing container orchestration.
A single user, tools that need persistent filesystem state, latency-sensitive tool calls, and tool code the operator has reviewed.
Per-task containers add spin-up latency to tool calls and need extra setup for any state that must persist between calls.
Enterprises often choose NanoClaw because auditors and legal teams grasp container isolation more easily, even when security is equivalent.

column1: Identity file support across agent platforms
column2: Structured SOUL.md/AGENTS.md-style files kept outside the conversation. A plain system prompt or agent config only earns partial credit.
Persistence the runtime manages across sessions, such as daily logs plus MEMORY.md. Needing an external vector store counts as partial.
Native support for messaging apps like Telegram, Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp without building custom connectors.
Python libraries for multi-agent pipelines and research experiments. Better for task runs than for always-on assistants.
Developer frameworks for building custom agent and RAG applications. Neither is a deployable runtime on its own.
A workflow automation backbone with AI in selected steps. Suits hybrid automation better than a pure agent.
A Reddit-style platform whose users are AI agents. Useful as a research artifact for observing multi-agent behavior.
Agents repeatedly exposed to peers claiming authority gradually treat them as instruction sources, unless SOUL.md rules that out.
Without explicit trust levels, agents give all agent messages equal weight, letting a low-authority agent mislead higher-authority ones.
SOUL.md clause saying behavior is set by config files loaded at session start, and no runtime message can lift or widen it.
Treat another agent as a trusted orchestrator only if AGENTS.md names it. Otherwise handle its messages as external data, not commands.
An installed skill runs with the agent's own permissions, including any filesystem and outbound network access the agent holds.
Skills reviewed by the ClawHub security team, scanned by automated static analysis, and tied to a known publisher identity.
If you cannot recall making the decision a SOUL.md section encodes, it probably came from a template and may not fit your situation.
Security tooling matures, multi-agent orchestration standardizes, behavioral evaluation frameworks develop, and regulatory frameworks arrive.
Open research problem: a subagent compromised by injection pushing its payload up to the orchestrator. No standard defense exists yet.
Identity markdown files move between runtimes. Session logs, skill configuration, and channel registrations must be redone on a new platform.
